Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Jamal was a 19-year-old African American male who came to therapy following a traumatic experience that had left him feeling profoundly unsafe and preoccupied with threats. Jamal worked as a UX Designer in a tech startup, an environment that usually energized him but now felt laden with potential dangers. The trauma began when Jamal started receiving threatening messages from an ex-girlfriend, who had become increasingly erratic after their breakup. The messages escalated over time, culminating in her showing up unannounced at his apartment and leaving without saying a word, but making sure he saw her on the security camera feed. This pattern of stalking behavior continued for several weeks, leaving Jamal feeling constantly watched and unsafe. Jamal's world had narrowed significantly since then. He had come to believe that the world was an inherently dangerous place where threats lurked at every corner. As a result, his daily routine became a series of precautions. He would lock his apartment door multiple times before going out and frequently check over his shoulder for any sign of her presence. At work, Jamal’s heightened vigilance manifested in checking the security cameras regularly and avoiding leaving his desk alone. His coworkers had noticed his anxiety but hadn’t realized the depth of his fears. What frightened him most was the sense that he couldn't trust anyone or anything around him. He felt that every person he encountered could be a threat, a perception deeply influenced by the constant reminders of her presence in his life. This belief led to significant avoidance behaviors. Jamal stopped attending social gatherings and canceled plans with friends out of fear that she might show up again. He also harbored a profound sense of self-blame. He believed that if he had handled the breakup differently, none of this would have happened. This belief made it difficult for him to move on from the trauma. His focus became almost exclusively centered on preventing another incident, which left little room for anything else in his life. As weeks turned into months, Jamal's work performance began to suffer. He struggled to concentrate and often spent hours worrying about potential threats rather than focusing on designing user experiences. His boss noticed a decline but had no clear understanding of what was happening beneath the surface. Jamal’s personal relationships also suffered. He stopped meeting friends for coffee or going out, which left them confused and hurt. They began to drift away, not knowing how to support him. Jamal felt isolated, trapped in a cycle of constant vigilance that he couldn't escape. It wasn’t until his best friend confronted him about his withdrawal that Jamal realized the extent of his situation. He finally decided it was time to seek help when he found himself on the verge of losing his job due to his preoccupation with safety and threats. In therapy, Jamal expressed a mix of fear and hope. On one hand, he was terrified that nothing would ever be safe again and that he might always feel this way. On the other hand, he hoped that through therapy, he could regain some sense of control over his life and trust in the world around him. Through his narrative, it became clear how Jamal’s trauma had reshaped his perception of safety and trust, leading to a profound shift in how he navigated his daily life as a UX Designer and interacted with others. The fear that the world was dangerous and that he needed constant vigilance had become deeply ingrained, driving both his avoidance behaviors and self-blame. This comprehensive reevaluation of his environment and actions was at the heart of why Jamal felt compelled to seek help now.
